note: Thirty invented, anonymised pieces of feedback with the cells a manager placed them on by hand. None is real feedback. `expected` lists every acceptable placement; an empty list means the framework does not cover it and the right answer is no suggestion.

items.content: During Tuesday's outage they took over the incident channel, posted updates every twenty minutes and kept the rest of us focused. Afterwards they wrote the follow-up actions and chased each one until it was done.
The billing migration slipped three weeks and I only heard about it in the sprint review. The work itself was solid, but the delay needed flagging much earlier.
Their reviews are the most useful on the team: they explain why something matters and usually suggest a concrete alternative rather than just pointing out the problem.
They spent most of this quarter pairing with our two new starters and both of them were shipping on their own within a month.
Great at the office quiz every Friday, and always remembers everyone's birthday.
Design and engineering were stuck on the onboarding flow for two weeks. They sat down with the designer, worked through the trade-offs and we left with a plan both sides were happy with.
The design doc for the new search index was hard to follow; product couldn't tell what we were trading off, and we had to run two extra meetings to explain it.
Instead of building the full export feature they suggested shipping a CSV download first to see whether anyone used it. Turned out only two customers did, which saved us weeks.
Tickets are picked up and finished on time, and when stuck they ask in the channel rather than waiting.
Pull requests often arrive without tests and need two or three rounds before they're ready to merge.
They led the payments rewrite across three teams, kept a clear plan of what landed when, and cut scope early when the risk became obvious. We shipped on the date we promised.
Noticed the nightly import job had been failing silently for a week. Nobody owned it, so they fixed it, added an alert and wrote down who owns it now.
In planning they sometimes dismiss other people's ideas before hearing them out, and a couple of the newer folk have stopped suggesting things.
Their weekly project updates are short, clear and say exactly what's at risk. Leadership started forwarding them as the example to follow.
On call last month they missed two pages overnight and the runbook steps weren't followed when they did respond.
Thanks for covering my shift at the help desk when my kid was sick!
They set up our team's review checklist and the linting rules, and the number of bugs reaching production dropped noticeably after that.
Two of the senior engineers on my team say their one-to-ones with them are the most useful hour of their week; one has since taken on tech lead duties.
Shipped the notifications redesign end to end: broke it into four releases, kept the board up to date and handled the edge cases without needing direction.
They built exactly what was in the ticket even when it was clear from the customer calls that the requirement didn't make sense. A quick question to product would have saved a rebuild.
Always happy to help when I'm stuck and asks good questions when they're stuck themselves.
After the release they kept checking the dashboards for a week, spotted a slow query nobody else had noticed and fixed it before customers complained.
Presented the case for moving off the legacy queue to the leadership group. Explained the cost, the risk and the alternatives in plain language, and got the budget approved in one meeting.
Review comments can come across as harsh; a few people now avoid asking them for reviews even though the feedback is usually right.
They reviewed my first big pull request line by line and then walked me through why each change mattered. I learned more in that hour than in my first month.
Commitments in standup regularly don't happen and I find out late. I need to be able to trust the dates you give.
The data and platform teams had been arguing about who owns the event schema for months. They got both leads in a room, wrote up the options and we finally have an agreed owner.
Brought really good snacks to the offsite.
A customer wrote in to thank the team after they joined a call, listened to the problem and proposed a small change that removed the customer's manual workaround.
Handled their first on-call week well: followed the runbook, escalated when it was outside what they knew and wrote a clear handover.
